title: Closed lifted-test evaluation identifies exchange for a nonaffine source
statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be a commutative condensed ring [sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring], with $\Lambda_T=p_T^*\Lambda$, exact module inverse images and ordinary unbounded internal module derived categories [sk-def-sfb-module-derived-pushpull, def-weil-size-convention]. Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $s:Z=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\hookrightarrow U$ a closed immersion, and $f:X\to U$ a qcqs morphism; $X$ need not be affine [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. Put $X_Z=X\times_UZ$ with projections $h:X_Z\to X$ and $f_Z:X_Z\to Z$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. On affine ind-etale bases let $v$ be the closed-site lift [def-exc-closed-site-lift]. Let $\mathscr T_s$ consist of affine ind-etale $V\to Z$ for which $V$ and $W=v(V)$ are w-contractible [sk-def-pe-wlocal]. These objects cover the affine ind-etale basis of $Z$; $V=W\times_UZ$, and if $W=\operatorname{Spec}B$ then $(B,IB)$ is a henselian pair, in particular $IB\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(B)$ [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Derived evaluation at the $V\in\mathscr T_s$ jointly detects isomorphisms. For $K\in D^+(\operatorname{Mod}_{\Lambda_X})$, set $T=X\times_UW$ and $T_0=X\times_UV$ with $b:T_0\hookrightarrow T$. There are canonical natural isomorphisms in $D(\mathbf{Ab})$
$$R\Gamma(V,s^*Rf_*K)\cong R\Gamma(T,K|_T),\qquad R\Gamma(V,R(f_Z)_*h^*K)\cong R\Gamma(T_0,b^*(K|_T)).$$
Under these isomorphisms the evaluated actual ambient exchange [def-weil-pbc-ambient-ringed-exchange] is precisely the canonical derived restriction $R\Gamma(T,K|_T)\to R\Gamma(T_0,b^*(K|_T))$, defined by the derived unit for $b$ and the direct-image composition comparison. The identifications are natural in $K$ and in test objects, commute with shifts and connecting maps, and are compatible with restriction to an affine open of a larger target. No invertibility of the restriction or exchange is asserted, and no finite presentation or properness of $f$ is assumed.

proof.text: Use the source-independent geometry and conservativity argument directly, without applying the aggregate affine exchange criterion. For any affine ind-etale object $V=\operatorname{Spec}\overline C$ of $Z$, the specified lift is $v(V)=\operatorname{Spec}H_A(\overline C)$. The closed-site functor theorem identifies its closed fibre with $V$, and the reduction theorem identifies the specified algebra map $C/IC\to\overline C$ as an isomorphism. The henselian-lift theorem applies to this very colimit algebra, so $(C,IC)$ is henselian. Consequently the w-contractibility equivalence for henselian quotients says that $V$ is w-contractible if and only if $v(V)$ is. This uses no finite generation of $I$. Let $V_0=\operatorname{Spec}B\to Z$ be an affine ind-etale object. Choose a faithfully flat ind-etale $B$-algebra $D$ that is w-contractible. Composition of ind-etale maps makes $\operatorname{Spec}D\to Z$ another affine ind-etale object, and faithful flatness makes $\operatorname{Spec}D\to V_0$ a pro-etale cover. Step 1 makes its specified closed lift w-contractible as well. Thus this cover belongs to $\mathscr T_s$. Since the affine ind-etale basis covers the full site, every site object is covered by tests from $\mathscr T_s$. Use the equivalence between internal modules and section-ring module sheaves, identical on underlying sheaves, sections and restriction maps. Exact evaluation at any w-contractible affine $V$ then applies to the internal modules here. For every unbounded complex $L$, the derived-section theorem identifies $R\Gamma(V,L)$ with its termwise section complex. Exactness gives $H^q(R\Gamma(V,L))=\Gamma(V,\mathcal H^qL)$: apply evaluation to the kernel defining cycles and the cokernel of boundaries. If all these derived sections vanish, each $\mathcal H^qL$ vanishes on all tests. For a section over any site object, restrict to a covering by tests from step 2; all restrictions are zero, so separatedness in the sheaf axiom makes the section zero. Thus every $\mathcal H^qL=0$. The map from the zero complex to a representative of $L$ is a quasi-isomorphism, hence $L=0$ in the derived localization. For a morphism $b$, apply this argument to its cone: evaluation is triangulated by exact-functor descent, so invertibility of every $R\Gamma(V,b)$ makes the evaluated cones zero, and hence the cone of $b$ zero. The distinguished-cone criterion makes $b$ invertible. This proves joint detection for unbounded objects without any convergence assertion. Fix an admissible V and put W=v(V). The closed-site functor theorem gives V=W×_U Z and specialization of every point of W into V. A maximal point of Spec B is closed, so it itself belongs to V; hence every maximal ideal contains IB and IB is contained in Jac(B). Fibre-product associativity gives T_0=X_Z×_X T=T×_W V and the indicated closed immersion b. This paragraph uses no exchange theorem; in particular it does not use lem-sfb-closed-test-derived-exchange-model.

proof.text: Use the equivalence between internal modules and modules over the section-ring sheaf, preserving underlying sheaves, sections and restrictions. Under the definition of module pushforward its underlying sections satisfy $(f_*F)(W)=F(X\times_UW)$; this formula has no affineness condition on $X$. The pullback is the lifted abelian inverse image with scalar extension along the specified coefficient isomorphism, so its underlying sheaf is the abelian inverse image, and its adjunction is the lifted one. We use the exactness of these module pullbacks stipulated in the statement. On any site object $T\to X$, condensed localization identifies $K|_T$ with literal slice restriction with transported coefficient action. Thus derived section localization applies to these internal-module functors and to nonaffine $T$.

source.place: Tag 09BL, transferred to the specified internal modules; section and slice conventions

proof.text: Fix the closed evaluation isomorphism to be the actual adjunction-unit section map $F(W)\to(s^*F)(V)$. Here is why this map is invertible, rather than just an unspecified natural isomorphism: geometric w-contractibility of $W$ makes evaluation at $W$ surjective on epimorphisms of set sheaves. The affine ind-etale basis comparison gives the same property for the identity basis object over $W$. Every point specializes into $V$ by step 1, so the closed-site counit theorem applied over $W$ makes that counit invertible. The specialization unit-comparison theorem then makes the actual unit section map invertible. This is the closed inverse-image evaluation of Tag 09BL (2). Apply this to underlying abelian sheaves; the lifted module adjunction of step 2 gives precisely this map on underlying groups. It is natural in $F$ and in the admissible tests, by the unit comparison and the ordinary unit-section definition.

source.place: Tags 09BK and 09BL (2); normalization by the actual closed-site unit

proof.text:
Choose a K-injective representative $I$ of $K$. The exact left adjoint $f^*$ ensures that $f_*I$ is K-injective, and it represents $Rf_*K$. Since evaluation at $V$ and $s^*$ are exact, step 3 and the direct-image section formula give canonical isomorphisms
$$R\Gamma(V,s^*Rf_*K)\cong Q((s^*f_*I)(V))\cong Q(I(T)).$$
Here $Q$ is localization of complexes of abelian groups. The derived section-localization theorem, applied to the object $T\to X$, identifies the last complex with $R\Gamma(T,K|_T)$ by the degreewise identity. The coefficient/slice identification is that of step 2. This constructs the first required isomorphism, with no affine-source hypothesis.

Choose a K-injective resolution $j:h^*I\to J$. Exactness of $h^*$ makes $J$ represent $h^*K$; the exact left adjoint $(f_Z)^*$ makes $(f_Z)_*J$ K-injective. As in step 4, exact evaluation at $V$ and section localization give
$$R\Gamma(V,R(f_Z)_*h^*K)\cong Q(J(T_0))\cong R\Gamma(T_0,(h^*K)|_{T_0}).$$
The localized ringed-site morphism for $h$ at $T\to X$ is $b:T_0\to T$. Its pullback comparison identifies $(h^*K)|_{T_0}\cong b^*(K|_T)$; the coefficient identification is the one from step 2. This gives the second required isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0D6F; localization of the ringed morphism h

proof.text: Compute the underived exchange on a module $F$. For $x\in F(T)=(f_*F)(W)$, the step-3 identification sends $x$ to its unit section $s^{-1}x$ in $(s^*f_*F)(V)$. Expand the exchange as unit for $f_Z$, pullback-composition comparison, and $h^*$ of the counit for $f$. In the sheafified Kan-extension description, the first two operations represent this section on $T_0$ by $x$ on $W$ and the map $T_0\to X\times_UW=T$. The counit sends a representative indexed by $W$ to its evaluation on $X\times_UW$. Consequently the resulting section is the inverse-image unit section of $x$ for $b:T_0\to T$. Equivalently the intermediate $f$-unit and $f$-counit cancel by the triangle identity. Thus the evaluated underived mate is $F(T)\to(b^*(F|_T))(T_0)$, the actual restriction map, including its specified coefficient action.

source.place: Tag 09BL (2), combined with the defining unit-square-counit formula for exchange

proof.text:
Apply step 6 degreewise to $I$ and then compose with $(f_Z)_*j$. The resulting chain map $s^*f_*I\to(f_Z)_*J$ represents the actual ambient derived exchange: under the canonical derived adjunction its transpose is $h^*\varepsilon_f$ followed by $j$, with the specified pullback comparison. The derived-adjunction theorem identifies this counit with the underived counit on $I$ and its resolution comparison, so uniqueness of adjoint transpose fixes the map. After exact evaluation at $V$, steps 3--6 identify it with
$$Q\bigl(I(T)\longrightarrow(h^*I)(T_0)\xrightarrow{j(T_0)}J(T_0)\bigr).$$
The first arrow is the localized unit section for $b$. No exactness of a closed direct image is used.

source.place: Tag 0D6F; derived adjunction applied to the normalized underived mate

proof.text: The map just displayed is exactly the unit-defined derived restriction. Indeed localized restriction takes $I$ and $J$ to K-injective complexes by K-injective restriction to a localized site, and the localized $j$ is a quasi-isomorphism from $b^*(I|_T)$ to $J|_{T_0}$. Hence the unit for $b^*\dashv Rb_*$ is computed by the ordinary unit followed by this resolution: the derived-adjunction theorem identifies the derived counit with the underived counit and the resolution comparison, and the derived unit is the unique map satisfying the triangle identities with that counit, which the ordinary unit followed by $b_*$ of the resolution does, since the underived unit and counit satisfy them. For sections and $b_*$, use the K-injective composition theorem: $b_*$ preserves K-injectives since $b^*$ is exact, and $\Gamma(T,b_*J)=\Gamma(T_0,J)$. The resulting composition comparison is the identity on these complexes. The derived universal transformation fixes this normalization; derived localization preserves the specified units and counits. Therefore the two isomorphisms of steps 4--5 carry the actual exchange to precisely the canonical derived restriction, as an equality in $D(\mathbf{Ab})$.

source.place: Tag 0D6F; derived restriction through the localized unit and canonical composition comparison

proof.text: Every morphism between derived inputs is represented by a unique homotopy class of maps between their K-injective representatives. Unit sections, the step-3 isomorphism, restriction and the chain maps in steps 4--8 commute with these maps. Each additive functor preserves chain homotopies. This proves naturality in $K$ and independence of the chosen resolutions. For a map $V'\to V$ of admissible tests, apply the naturality of the unit-section comparison and the presheaf restriction maps $I(T)\to I(T')$ and $J(T_0)\to J(T'_0)$: the displayed chain map commutes because adjunction units are sheaf morphisms. The identities are degreewise, so replacing $I$ by $I[n]$ gives the same equalities under the standard shift comparisons. The exchange commutes with connecting morphisms by its canonical triangulated compatibility; the section identifications, being these natural chain comparisons, have the same compatibility.

source.place: Tag 0D6F; natural chain comparisons and the canonical shift structures

proof.text: If the square is obtained by restriction to an affine open of a larger target, localize the larger square at that open. The ringed localization theorem identifies the localized direct images and pullbacks with those of this square, compatibly with the specified derived units and counits. Section localization uses the identity on the same restricted complexes. Thus the maps in steps 4--8 are the restrictions of the corresponding maps before localizing; in particular the unit-section map of step 6 is unchanged on the test fibre products. This proves the requested open-target compatibility. All calculations allow empty tests, the zero coefficient ring, and $K=0$. If $I=0$, the closed inverse image and restriction are identities; if $I=A$, the target is empty and its derived section complexes are zero. No step uses properness or finite presentation of $f$, nor claims that restriction is invertible.

source.place: Tag 0D6F; naturality of localization and of the derived adjunction units and counits

proof.text: For the proved nonaffine_test_naturality declaration, apply proetale_section_localization to f on the lifted test and to fZ on V; their TestNaturality conclusions give the first two conjuncts. Apply closed_derived_evaluation to each K.obj for the third conjunct. Pro-affine-etale structure maps are weakly etale. The ambient normalization and main identification remain open with the preceding source plan.
